catalog_quote: [McGregor 2011: 98 n. 18] Stress is scarcely discussed in the earlier literature on Nyulnyul. The only place where I am aware of any mention is in Nekes & Worms (2006:67), where there is an exceedingly brief discussion of ‘accentuation’ amounting to less than half a page. It is stated that accent—one infers in the standard average Australian language—falls on the first syllable of a word, and sometimes a secondary accent falls on the fourth syllable. A few illustrative examples are given in Nyulnyul. The facts, as will be seen in this section, are much more complicated than this. [Nekes & Worms 2006: 67, Google Books snippet fragments, not one continuous run:] Accentuation The main accent of a word usually falls on the first syllable ... fourth syllable of the word yámendedjàlen.78 Another example illustrating secondary accent is provided by the Nyikina mindenàno ‘you told me’, with secondary accent on the third syllable. The secondary accent in this case can be explained as the result of the fact that this word represents the contraction of two words mindena ‘you told’ and ... accentuation explained in the introduction.80 In these few exceptions we employ the usage of grave and acute diacritics, as proposed by the Smithsonian Institute ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Main word accent on the first syllable, with an occasional secondary accent on the fourth syllable — a blanket statement Nekes & Worms make for the Kimberley (Dampier Land) languages they describe, which include Dyao/Jawi, illustrated with Nyulnyul (and some Bardi) words. It matches the first-hand Bardi statement (Bowern, McDonough & Kelliher 2012: 343, held by the project: 'Primary stress is regular and appears consistently on the initial syllable of the word'), and Bowern treats Jawi as a mutually intelligible dialect of Bardi.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nekes & Worms (per McGregor): 'sometimes a secondary accent falls on the fourth syllable'. For Bardi (JIPA 2012: 343-344) secondary stress is complex: third syllable in trisyllables (always heavy), third or fourth in tetrasyllables depending on weight, plus morphologically assigned stress on verb roots and heavy affixes/clitics. Bowern 2012 (snippet) notes a Jawi-only lenition of the velar nasal 'in non-post-stress positions', which presupposes the same stress placement in Jawi.
new_statements.exceptions: Nekes & Worms snippet mentions 'few exceptions' handled by an accentuation convention 'explained in the introduction' (wording cut off in the snippet); McGregor 2011 says the Nyulnyul facts 'are much more complicated than this'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement for isolated words (accentuation of dictionary/example forms); no Jawi-specific data. Nothing about phrase-level accent for Jawi.
new_statements.identity_note: Jawi/Djawi [djaw1238] is treated by Bowern (2008: 60; JIPA 2012: 333; Grammar of Bardi 2012) as a mutually intelligible dialect of Bardi [bard1255] (three named varieties: Bardi, Baard, Jawi); Glottolog keeps it as a separate language. Every stress statement located is either family-level (Nekes & Worms 2006: 67; Crowley & Bowern 2010 exercise note) or Bardi-level (Bowern 2012 grammar §5.1; Bowern, McDonough & Kelliher 2012: 343). The only Jawi-specific remark touching stress is Bowern 2012's Jawi velar-nasal lenition 'in non-post-stress positions' (snippet). Recommend the catalog treat djaw1238 as covered by the Bardi entry (initial stress) with a dialect note rather than as an independent description.

sources.citation: McGregor, William B. (2011). The Nyulnyul language of Dampier Land, Western Australia. Pacific Linguistics 632. Canberra: ANU. p. 98 n. 18.
sources.note: Reports second-hand that Nekes & Worms (2006:67) have a half-page on 'accentuation' stating that accent 'falls on the first syllable of a word, and sometimes a secondary accent falls on the fourth syllable', with Nyulnyul examples; McGregor infers the statement is meant for 'the standard average Australian language'. Nekes & Worms's coverage includes Dyao (= Jawi).

sources.note: Nothing on stress.
